title: DSA in Python: arrays and hashing
seriesDescription: Hashing, windows, stacks, binary search, lists, trees, heaps and graphs with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Python hashing for interviews: dict, Counter and defaultdict idioms, hashable keys, prefix sums, anagram grouping and expected versus worst-case cost.
source: Python documentation (dict, collections.Counter, defaultdict, data model: hashable); LeetCode two sum, group anagrams and subarray sum equals K; Cracking the Coding Interview

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `two_sum(nums, target)` that returns the indices of two different elements adding up to target in one pass using a `dict` (assume exactly one answer exists).

checks.label: uses a dict from value to index
looks up the complement target - x
stores each value with its index

questions.explanation: Check the dict before inserting the current element, otherwise `[3, 2, 4]` with `target 6` pairs index 0 with itself. Other correct solutions (a `get` call, a fill-first pass) also pass.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `group_anagrams(strs)` that returns the words grouped so that anagrams share a group. Use a dictionary keyed by the sorted letters.

checks.label: uses a dict that groups lists (defaultdict, setdefault or get)
builds a key from the sorted characters
joins or tuples the sorted letters into a hashable key
appends each word to its group

questions.explanation: A list cannot be a dict key, so join or tuple the sorted letters. A tuple of 26 counts also works and is faster for long words.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `longest_consecutive(nums)` returning the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like `3,4,5,6`) present in an unsorted list, in O(n) expected time using a `set`.

checks.label: puts the numbers in a set
only starts counting at a number whose predecessor is absent
extends the run with a loop

questions.explanation: Starting only at run beginnings means each element is visited at most twice overall, so it is O(n) expected despite the nested loop. Sorting is O(n log n) and acceptable as a first answer, but the question asks for O(n).

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `subarray_sum(nums, k)` that counts the contiguous subarrays whose sum equals `k`. The list may contain negative numbers, so aim for O(n) with a `dict` of prefix-sum counts.

checks.label: uses a dict (or Counter) of prefix-sum counts
seeds the counts with prefix 0 occurring once

questions.model:
from collections import defaultdict

def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    seen = defaultdict(int)
    seen[0] = 1
    prefix = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        count += seen[prefix - k]
        seen[prefix] += 1
    return count
questions.explanation: Because values can be negative a sliding window does not work. Counting before recording the current prefix keeps a zero-length subarray from being counted. With a `defaultdict`, reading `seen[prefix - k]` inserts a zero entry; `seen.get(prefix - k, 0)` avoids that.

questions.prompt: Match each Python expression with what it does.

right.text: Reads the value, or 0 when the key is missing, without inserting anything
Inserts an empty list when the key is missing and returns the stored list
Builds a mapping from each element to how often it occurs
A dict whose missing keys are created on first access as new empty lists
Removes the key if present and returns its value, or `None` when it is missing
Locks the entry so other threads cannot change it

questions.explanation: `get` avoids a `KeyError`, `setdefault` and `defaultdict` build multi-maps, `Counter` counts, and `pop` with a default never raises.

questions.text: To count items, build a {1}(items) from collections and call .{2}(k) for the k most frequent; to group values by key, use a {3}(list) and append to each key's list.
questions.explanation: `Counter` and `defaultdict` remove the "`if key not in d`" boilerplate. `most_common(k)` uses a heap internally when k is given.

questions.prompt: How many keys does the dict `{1: "a", True: "b", 1.0: "c"}` contain after it is built?
questions.explanation: The values `1, True and 1.0` are equal and have the same hash, so they are the same key; the later values overwrite the stored value but the first key object stays. I ran it: `len` is 1. Bring this up when a key mixes bool and int.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A `dict`-based two sum is guaranteed O(n) time even in the worst case.
questions.reason: Dict lookups and inserts take O(1) time on average.

whys.a: A is not true as stated, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so option c cannot hold.
whys.d: Correct: O(1) is an average-case (expected) bound. Many colliding keys can degrade lookups towards O(n), so the worst case is not O(n).

questions.explanation: Say "expected O(n)" in an interview. It shows you know the difference between expected and worst-case hash costs.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Grouping anagrams with the key `"".join(sorted(word))` costs O(n * k log k) for n words of length k.
questions.reason: Sorting the k characters of one word takes O(k) time.

whys.a: R is false, so this cannot be right.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option holds.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (n sorts of cost k log k) but comparison sorting k characters takes O(k log k), not O(k).
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: The alternative key is a `26-count tuple`, giving O(n * k) for lowercase words. Mention both.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A `list` cannot be used as a dict key, but a `tuple` of the same numbers can.
questions.reason: Lists are mutable and therefore unhashable, while a `tuple` of hashable items is immutable and hashable.

whys.a: Correct: a hashable object must keep the same hash for life; mutable lists cannot promise that.
whys.b: R is exactly the reason, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Convert a list to a `tuple` (or a string) before using it as a key or putting it in a set. A tuple that contains a list is still unhashable.

questions.prompt: This Python two sum inserts first and then checks: `for i, x in enumerate(nums): seen[x] = i; if target - x in seen: return [seen[target - x], i]`. What does it return for `nums = [3, 2, 4]`, `target = 6`?

options.why: Correct: after storing `3` at index 0 the lookup of 6 - 3 finds index 0 straight away.

options.text: `[1, 2], the correct pair of the values 2 and 4`
options.why: That needs the `check` to run before the insert; this order never gets there.

options.text: None, because no pair of values sums to 6
options.why: The pair 2 and 4 exists, and the function returns earlier anyway.

options.text: A `KeyError` raised on the very first iteration
options.why: The code tests with `in` before indexing, so a missing key is never read.

questions.explanation: Look up the complement before storing the current value. This is the classic "use the same element twice" bug. I ran it: the result is `[0, 0]`.

questions.prompt: Python's `Counter.most_common(k)` is implemented with a heap, so selecting the top k of n distinct keys costs about O(n log k) rather than a full sort.

options.why: Correct: with an argument it uses `heapq.nlargest`; without one it sorts everything.
It does use a heap when k is given.

questions.explanation: Top-K frequent: count with a `dict` (O(n)), then a size-k heap (O(n log k)) or bucket sort by frequency (O(n)).

questions.prompt: Which statements about Python `dict` are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Iteration follows insertion order, a guaranteed language feature since Python 3.7.
options.why: Correct: the order of insertion is part of the language, not just CPython.
Correct: lists, sets and dicts cannot be keys, but tuples of hashables can.
False: it raises `KeyError`; use `d.get(k)` for None.

options.text: Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average.
options.why: Correct: that is the average (expected) cost of a hash table.

questions.explanation: Know the contracts: ordered, hashable keys, KeyError on missing, average O(1).
